meta.title: Column Depot — Learn ClickHouse
meta.description: A warehouse game that teaches how ClickHouse really stores and reads data: columns, parts, merges, the sparse index and partitions. Unofficial.

objective.insert: Insert orders: every truck brings one sealed section (a part).
objective.query: Pick the columns, then run the query: Pico only walks the aisles you ask for.
objective.again: Try reading more or fewer columns and watch the counter.

panel.title: What Pico read
panel.hintInsert: The depot is empty. Send a truck with orders first.
panel.hintQuery: Choose which columns the query needs and press Run.
panel.verdict: {pct}% of the bytes: the query names {cols} of {all} columns, so the other aisles were never opened.

level.noPeeking: The depot is hidden on purpose: remembering it from memory is what makes it stick.
level.remedial: You need 80% to unlock the next level. Try again: the questions change their numbers.

panels.noQuery: No query yet. Pick columns and press Run.
panels.partsMeterNote: Here: slow down at {delay}, reject at {throw}. Real ClickHouse: 1000 and 3000 per partition.

1-1.title: Rows vs columns
1-1.summary: Why reading one column of a row store means opening everything.

brief.title: The orders depot
brief.body: Hi! I'm Pico, the picker robot at Column Depot. We store millions of orders here: each one has a date, a customer, a city and a total. Right now we store them like most databases do: by rows. Every box holds whole orders, with their four values packed together. The coloured sticker on each box tells you which column it holds.
brief.breaks: A box isn't a real object: it's a chunk of a file on disk. “Opening” a box means reading it and decompressing it.

map.block: a block of data on disk

rowSum.q: A ticket arrives: add up every order's total. The boxes hold whole rows. How many of the {n} boxes will Pico have to open?
rowSum.quarter: A quarter: only the total ones
rowSum.why: All of them. In a row store each order's total is packed next to its date, customer and city, so to add up one column you open everything.

rotate.title: Let's rotate the depot
rotate.body: Now we reorganise: every aisle will hold a single column. Watch every box fly to its aisle by its sticker. This is what ClickHouse does on disk: one file per column.

colSum.q: Same ticket, same {total} boxes, now stored by column. How many boxes does Pico open to add up the totals?
colSum.why: Only the {n} in the total aisle: the other aisles aren't even touched. That's a columnar database: each column in its own file, and a query reads only the columns it names.

byCity.title: Revenue by city
byCity.body: Your first ticket: revenue per city, SELECT city, sum(total) … GROUP BY city. Pick exactly the columns it needs and run it.
byCity.success: Two aisles out of four, half the boxes. You only paid for what you asked for.

together.q: In a columnar database, what is stored together?
together.column: All the values of one column
together.row: All the values of one row
together.random: Whatever arrived at the same time
together.why: Each column lives in its own file, so a query can read just the columns it needs.

files.q: A ClickHouse table has 100 columns. A query uses {n} of them. How many column files does it read?
files.why: {n}: one file per column it names. The other columns are never opened.

rowStore.q: A row store keeps whole rows in {n} boxes. You add up one column. How many boxes do you open?
rowStore.why: All {n}: every box has a bit of every column, so you can't read one column alone.

shines.q: Which query does column storage make fast?
shines.aggregate: Add up one column over millions of rows
shines.lookup: Fetch one whole row by its id
shines.update: Change one field of one row
shines.why: Aggregating a few columns over many rows: you read only those columns. Fetching or updating single rows is what row stores are built for.

1-2.title: Only what you ask for
1-2.summary: The columns a query names decide the bytes it reads.

brief.title: Every column costs
brief.body: Now the depot is stored by column. The rule is simple: a query reads only the columns it names. Columns don't all weigh the same either: a long number takes more bytes than a short city code. The panel on the right counts the bytes read.

star.q: Someone sends SELECT *. What share of the depot's bytes does Pico read?
star.why: 100%: the star means every column, so Pico walks every aisle. SELECT * throws away the main advantage of a columnar database.

lightest.q: Which one-column query reads the fewest bytes?
lightest.why: city: it's a LowCardinality(String), a few cities repeated over and over, so on disk it's tiny. Same number of boxes, very different weight.

daily.title: Daily sales
daily.body: Ticket: sales per day, SELECT date, sum(total) … GROUP BY date. Pick exactly its columns and run it.
daily.success: Date and total, nothing else. The other aisles stayed closed.

unique.title: Unique customers per city
unique.body: Ticket: how many different customers each city has, SELECT city, uniq(customer_id) … GROUP BY city.
unique.success: Exactly the columns it needs. Watch the bytes: customer_id weighs much more than city.

star.q: SELECT * on a table with {n} columns: how many columns does it read?
star.why: {n}: all of them. Name your columns.

unnamed.q: What happens to the columns a query doesn't name?
unnamed.why: They're never opened: each column is a separate file on disk.

pct.q: A query reads {read} of {of} columns that all weigh the same. What percentage of the bytes does it read?

sizes.q: Do all columns weigh the same on disk?
sizes.differ: No: it depends on the type and how well it compresses
sizes.same: Yes, every column takes the same
sizes.why: They differ: types have different sizes, and repetitive data compresses much better.

1-3.title: Shrinking aisles
1-3.summary: Each column is compressed on its own; sorting makes it shrink more.

brief.title: Squeeze every aisle
brief.body: Each column is compressed on its own. Values of the same column look alike, so they compress far better than mixed rows. And when equal values sit side by side (if the table is sorted by that column), they shrink even more. The ratios here are illustrative; the rule is real.

squeeze.title: Compression
squeeze.body: Watch every aisle shrink. city has few distinct values and shrinks a lot; total barely changes, because almost every total is different.

sortCity.q: If we sort the table by city (ORDER BY city), which aisle shrinks the most?
sortCity.why: city: all the Limas end up together, then all the Madrids… long runs of the same value compress almost to nothing.

smallest.title: The smallest depot
smallest.body: Try different ORDER BY columns and leave the one that makes the whole table smallest. Watch the total at the bottom of the panel.
smallest.success: customer_id wins here: it was the column that compressed worst, so sorting it saves the most bytes. Choosing the ORDER BY is choosing what gets compressed, and (World 3) what gets read fast.

why.q: Why does a column compress better than a row?
why.alike: Its values have the same type and look alike
why.why: Similar values side by side: compressors love repetition.

sorted.q: Sorting the table by a column makes that column…
sorted.why: Equal values end up next to each other, forming long runs.

codecSmall.q: ClickHouse 26.9, no CODEC clause: what does a freshly inserted {mb} MB part use?
codecSmall.why: LZ4: since 26.9 parts under 100 MB use LZ4 and parts from 100 MB use ZSTD(3).

codecBig.q: ClickHouse 26.9, no CODEC clause: what does a {mb} MB merged part use?
codecBig.why: ZSTD(3): parts of 100 MB or more use ZSTD(3) since 26.9 (before, LZ4 everywhere; Cloud uses ZSTD).

1-4.title: Analytics, not a ticket window
1-4.summary: What ClickHouse is built for, and what it isn't.

brief.title: OLAP vs OLTP
brief.body: ClickHouse is an analytical (OLAP) database: it's built to scan and aggregate millions of rows over a few columns. A shop's checkout, a login or updating one order every second are transactional (OLTP) work: rows read and written one by one. For that, a database like Postgres is the right tool.

lookup.q: A clerk asks for one whole order: SELECT * … WHERE customer_id = 420. In how many aisles does Pico have to open boxes?
lookup.why: 4: one whole row is spread over the 4 aisles, so Pico visits them all (and reads entire boxes of 8,192 rows to return one). A row store would open a single box. Single-row lookups are OLTP territory.

yearly.q: The boss wants yearly revenue: SELECT sum(total). What share of the boxes does Pico open?
yearly.why: 25%: one aisle out of four, over every row. That's the kind of question ClickHouse answers in milliseconds.

light.title: A featherweight report
light.body: Orders per city and day: SELECT …, count() with at least two columns that reads under 10% of the bytes. Which pair is light enough?
light.success: date and city: both repeat a lot and compress very well. Picking light columns is half of a fast report.

real.title: The real thing
real.body: This is the depot in real ClickHouse. system.columns tells you how much each column weighs on disk, compressed and uncompressed.

fits.dashboard: A dashboard aggregating billions of events
fits.cart: A shopping cart updated on every click
fits.login: Checking one user's password at login
fits.why: Aggregating huge amounts of data. Carts and logins read and write single rows: OLTP.

oneRow.q: To read one whole row of a {n}-column table, how many column files does ClickHouse touch?
oneRow.why: {n}: the row is spread over every column file.

minimum.q: What is the smallest amount ClickHouse reads from a column?
minimum.why: A granule: the index points to blocks of 8,192 rows, never to single rows. You'll see it in World 3.

updates.q: You need to update one order's status every second. Where?
updates.why: In an OLTP database. ClickHouse parts are immutable; changing single rows is expensive (World 6).

2-1.title: One truck, one section
2-1.summary: Every INSERT becomes a new, immutable part.

brief.title: Every insert is a part
brief.body: Every INSERT arrives like a truck and becomes a new sealed section on the shelves: a part. A part is immutable: once written, ClickHouse never edits it. Its name says where it comes from: partition_minBlock_maxBlock_level. Without PARTITION BY, the partition is called all.
brief.breaks: A part isn't furniture: it's a folder on disk with one file per column, its marks and its index.

two.title: Two deliveries
two.body: Send two trucks of orders. Watch each one become its own section, with its own label.
two.success: Two inserts, two parts: all_1_1_0 and all_2_2_0. Block 1, block 2, level 0 (never merged).

third.q: A third truck arrives. What will its part be called?
third.why: all_3_3_0: block number 3 (from 3 to 3) and level 0, because it hasn't been merged with anything yet.

fix.q: An order inside all_1_1_0 has a wrong total. What does ClickHouse do with that part?
fix.newPart: It never edits it: any change writes a new part
fix.edit: It edits the row in place
fix.appendRow: It appends the fix at the end of the file
fix.why: Parts are immutable. Changes are always new parts (mutations, lightweight updates) that replace the old ones later. You'll see the costs in World 4 and beyond.

real.title: The real thing
real.body: In real ClickHouse you see the parts in system.parts: name, rows and level of each active one.

name.q: No merges yet. What is the part of the {k}th insert called?

immutable.q: When does ClickHouse modify an existing part?
immutable.why: Never. Parts are immutable; new data and changes are always new parts.

oneRow.q: An INSERT of a single row creates…
oneRow.row: one more row in the last part
oneRow.why: A whole part, with its files. That's why row-by-row inserts are a problem (level 2-3).

level.q: What does the last number of all_1_1_0 mean?
level.merges: How many merges deep it is (level)
level.why: The level: 0 for a fresh insert, and it goes up with every merge.

2-2.title: The press
2-2.summary: Background merges fuse neighbouring parts into bigger ones.

brief.title: Merges in the background
brief.body: Many small parts are slow to read. So ClickHouse runs merges in the background: it takes neighbouring parts of the same partition, sorts their rows together and writes one bigger part. The new name joins the block ranges and adds 1 to the level. The old parts become outdated and are deleted about 8 minutes later (old_parts_lifetime = 480 s).

first.title: The first merge
first.body: Watch the press come down on all_1_1_0 and all_2_2_0. Two parts go in, one comes out.

next.q: Now the press fuses all_1_2_1 with all_3_3_0. What's the new part called?

gap.q: Could the press fuse all_1_3_2 with a part all_5_5_0 while all_4_4_0 sits between them?
gap.no: No: merges only take a contiguous run of parts
gap.fill: Yes, and it leaves a gap
gap.why: No. A merge takes neighbouring parts (consecutive block ranges) of one partition, so the name always describes one continuous range.

work.title: Let the press work
work.body: Send a few trucks. You don't have to do anything else: the press merges on its own, whenever it decides.
work.success: Nobody pressed OPTIMIZE: merges run continuously in the background. Big parts stop growing around 150 GiB.

name.why: {name}: the block ranges join and the level is the highest + 1.

lifetime.q: After a merge, when are the old parts deleted?
lifetime.why: They linger as outdated for 480 s, just in case, then go.

contiguous.q: Can a merge combine two parts that have another part between them?
contiguous.why: No: merges take consecutive parts of one partition.

optimize.why: They're automatic. OPTIMIZE … FINAL exists but is rarely needed (and expensive).

2-3.title: Too many parts
2-3.summary: Row-by-row inserts make parts faster than merges can fuse them.

brief.title: The afternoon rush
brief.body: An app sends one order per INSERT, several times a second. Every insert is a part, and the press can only fuse so fast. In real ClickHouse, when one partition has 1000 active parts inserts slow down, and at 3000 they're rejected: Too many parts. This depot is small, so here the limits are 5 and 15.

rush.title: Survive the rush
rush.body: Keep the depot below the slow-down line for 8 seconds in a row. The app sends tiny inserts; the press is already working flat out. What can you change?
rush.success: Batches did it: fewer, bigger inserts, and the press keeps up. The recommendation is 10,000–100,000 rows per INSERT and about one INSERT per second.

math.q: An app sends 50 single-row inserts per second and merges remove 40 parts per second. Starting from 0, how many seconds until the real limit of 3000 parts?
math.why: The parts grow by 50 − 40 = 10 per second: 3000 / 10 = 300 seconds. Five minutes and the inserts start failing.

real.title: The real fix
real.body: Don't raise the limit: fix the cause. Batch your inserts, or let the server batch them for you with async inserts (next level).

limits.q: Real ClickHouse: at how many active parts per partition does it slow down and then reject inserts?

scope.why: Per partition (plus a table-wide cap of 100,000 parts).

fix.q: You get “Too many parts”. What's the right fix?
fix.batch: Bigger, less frequent inserts (or async inserts)
fix.why: Batching. Raising the limit hides the problem, and more partitions make it worse.

time.q: {ins} single-row inserts per second, merges remove {mer} parts per second. Seconds until 3000 parts?

2-4.title: Batches & async inserts
2-4.summary: The server can batch small inserts for you.

brief.title: Let the server batch
brief.body: Sometimes you can't batch: hundreds of small clients send a row each. With async inserts the server keeps those rows in a buffer and writes one part when the first limit is hit: 200 ms (adaptive), 10 MiB or 450 queries. Since 26.2 it's on by default (async_insert = 1). In this depot, time runs slower: the buffer flushes every 2 seconds.

clients.title: A swarm of tiny clients
clients.body: Hundreds of clients, one tiny insert each. Keep the depot below the slow-down line for 8 seconds in a row.
clients.success: The hopper collected the rows and flushed one part at a time. Same data, a fraction of the parts.

rate.q: 200 single-row inserts per second, with async inserts flushing every 200 ms. How many parts per second?
rate.why: One part per flush: 1000 ms / 200 ms = 5 parts per second, instead of 200.

fire.q: Someone sets wait_for_async_insert = 0 to go faster. What do they risk?
fire.lost: The client never learns if the flush failed: errors only reach the server logs
fire.why: It's fire-and-forget: if the flush fails, the client already got an OK. The docs recommend async_insert = 1 with wait_for_async_insert = 1.

real.title: The real settings
real.body: These are the defaults since 26.2. ClickHouse Cloud uses a bigger buffer (100 MiB) and a longer timeout.

default.why: On: async_insert = 1 by default since 26.2 (some docs pages still say otherwise).

first.q: Clients send 1 KB inserts, 100 per second. Which flush limit is hit first?
first.why: Time: in 200 ms only about 20 inserts (20 KB) arrive, far from 10 MiB or 450 queries.

wait.lost: Errors go unnoticed by the client
wait.why: Fire-and-forget: a failed flush only shows up in the server logs.

batch.q: Recommended batch size for synchronous inserts?
batch.why: 10k–100k rows per INSERT, about one INSERT per second.

2-5.title: Case: the truck that came twice
2-5.summary: Insert deduplication drops a retried block.

brief.title: A new case!
brief.body: A client swears they sent a block of orders once. The network failed before the OK arrived, so their program retried. Will the orders be duplicated? ClickHouse keeps a hash of every inserted block: if the exact same block comes back inside the window, it's ignored. Replicated tables and Cloud do it by default; plain MergeTree only if you set non_replicated_deduplication_window. Our depot has it on.

retry.title: Retry the delivery
retry.body: Send block B-17, then retry it exactly as it was. Watch what the dock does with the second truck.
retry.success: The retry was turned away: same block, same hash. Safe retries are why deduplication exists.

changed.q: Objection! The client edits one order inside B-17 and retries. What happens?
changed.inserted: It's inserted: a different block has a different hash
changed.why: Inserted, because deduplication compares whole blocks. Now the unchanged orders exist twice. Retry the exact same block, or use an insert_deduplication_token.

diagnose.q: Second witness: a dashboard app inserts one row at a time and the parts keep piling up. Your verdict?
diagnose.async: Turn on async inserts or batch the rows
diagnose.why: Batching (by the client or the server). Raising the limit or partitioning more only makes it worse.

verdict.q: Final question: two different INSERTs each contain order 4200. How many copies end up in the table?
verdict.one: One: the primary key is unique
verdict.why: Both. Deduplication is per block, not per key, and the primary key isn't unique (World 3). Removing duplicate rows is another tool: ReplacingMergeTree.

what.block: the hash of the whole inserted block
what.why: The block's hash: it makes retries safe, it doesn't dedupe rows.

window.w10k: The last 10,000 blocks, up to 1 hour

plain.q: On a plain (non-replicated) MergeTree, insert deduplication is by default…
plain.why: Off: non_replicated_deduplication_window = 0 unless you set it.

notUnique.q: Two different blocks contain the same order. Result?
notUnique.why: Both: different blocks have different hashes.

3-1.title: Boxes of 8192
3-1.summary: The granule: the smallest thing ClickHouse reads.

brief.title: Granules
brief.body: Inside each part, rows are sorted by the ORDER BY and cut into granules of up to 8192 rows (index_granularity). One box is one granule of one column. ClickHouse never reads a single row: the smallest thing it reads is a whole granule.
brief.breaks: 8192 is a maximum: with very wide rows a granule can hold fewer (index_granularity_bytes = 10 MiB).

map.granule: a granule (≤ 8192 rows of one column)
map.orderBy: rows sorted by ORDER BY inside the part

count.q: A part has 100,000 rows. How many granules?
count.why: 100,000 / 8192 = 12.2 → 13 granules (the last one is partly full).

oneRow.q: WHERE customer_id = 4200 matches a single order. At least how many rows does ClickHouse read?
oneRow.why: A whole granule: the index points to granules, not to rows. That's the price of a tiny index.

find.title: Find customer 777
find.body: The query already filters WHERE customer_id = 777. Pick its column and run it: Pico should open a single granule per column.
find.success: One granule: the table is sorted by customer_id, so the index knew exactly where to look.

unit.q: What is the smallest unit ClickHouse reads?
unit.why: A granule (of each column it needs).

sorted.q: The rows are sorted by ORDER BY…
sorted.why: Inside each part. Different parts overlap until they're merged.

3-2.title: The board at the entrance
3-2.summary: A sparse index: one entry per granule.

brief.title: The sparse index
brief.body: At the entrance there's a board: primary.idx. It has one entry per granule: the key of the granule's first row. It's tiny (the docs' table: 8.87 million rows, 1083 entries, 97 KiB), so it lives in memory. To find a key, ClickHouse does a binary search on the board and reads only the granules that can contain it.

search.title: Looking up a customer
search.body: Watch the board on the right: for customer 5100 only one entry can match, and Pico goes straight to that box.

entries.q: A part has 1083 granules. How many entries does its primary.idx have?
entries.why: 1083: one per granule. That's why it's called sparse.

holds.q: What does the primary index store?
holds.first: The key values of each granule's first row
holds.offsets: Byte offsets in the column files
holds.why: The first key of each granule. Offsets live in the marks files (one per column), which tell ClickHouse where each granule starts.

lean.title: The leanest lookup
lean.body: Read only the total of customer 3100. Aim for the minimum: one granule of the filter column plus one of total.
lean.success: 2 boxes out of 72: the filter column (to check) and total (the answer).

entries.q: The primary index has one entry per…

marks.q: What do the marks files store?
marks.offsets: Where each granule starts in a column file
marks.why: Offsets (compressed block, offset inside it) so a reader can jump to granule N.

size.q: A part has {g} granules. How many primary-index entries?

memory.q: Where does the primary index live?
memory.why: In memory (loaded lazily since 24.2): it's a few KiB per million rows.

3-3.title: Second in line
3-3.summary: The order of the key columns decides what can be skipped.

brief.title: Two columns in the key
brief.body: With ORDER BY (a, b) the data is sorted by a, and by b only inside each value of a. A filter on a uses binary search. A filter on b can only skip a granule when a is constant inside it. In the docs: first column → 1 of 1083 granules; second column → 1076 of 1083. So put the low-cardinality column first.

cityFirst.q: ORDER BY (customer_id, city): how many of the 24 granules does WHERE city = 'Lima'' read?
cityFirst.why: All 24: each granule mixes many customers, so city takes every value in every granule. The index can't rule anything out.

swap.q: Same data with ORDER BY (city, customer_id). How many granules now?
swap.why: 4: all the Limas sit together, so only Lima's granules are read.

daily.title: The daily reports
daily.body: Two reports run every day: one by city, one by customer. Choose the key and run both: together they must read 10 granules or fewer.
daily.success: City first: 4 + 6 = 10 granules. Customer first would be 24 + 1 = 25. Low cardinality first helps the second column too.

rule.q: Which column usually goes first in ORDER BY?
rule.low: The one with fewer distinct values
rule.why: Low cardinality first: it keeps later columns prunable and compresses better.

docs.q: Docs: 1/1083 granules for one filter, 1076/1083 for another. Which filtered the second key column?
docs.why: The second column barely prunes when the first has high cardinality.

when.q: When can a filter on the 2nd key column skip a granule?
when.constant: When the 1st column is constant inside it
when.why: Only then is the 2nd column's range in that granule meaningful (generic exclusion search).

notInKey.q: A filter on a column that isn't in the key reads…
notInKey.why: The primary index can't help; skipping indexes might (World 7).

3-4.title: The key isn't unique
3-4.summary: PRIMARY KEY sorts and indexes; it doesn't forbid duplicates.

brief.title: Not a uniqueness rule
brief.body: In Postgres a primary key is unique. In ClickHouse it isn't: PRIMARY KEY only decides what goes into the sparse index. By default it's the ORDER BY; if you set it, it must be a prefix of the ORDER BY. Two rows with the same key happily coexist.

twice.q: You insert another batch that also contains orders of customer 4200 (same key). How many parts hold customer 4200 now?
twice.one: One: the old row is replaced
twice.why: Two. Nobody checks uniqueness; the new part simply has its own copy.

both.title: Find both copies
both.body: Read customer 4200: Pico has to visit both sections.
both.success: One granule in each part. Removing duplicates is a job for ReplacingMergeTree (a later world).

prefix.why: Invalid: PRIMARY KEY must be a prefix of ORDER BY, so it could be city or (city, customer_id), not customer_id.

real.title: PRIMARY KEY vs ORDER BY
real.body: A shorter PRIMARY KEY makes the index smaller while the data stays sorted by the full ORDER BY.

unique.q: Does a ClickHouse PRIMARY KEY enforce uniqueness?
unique.why: No. It's a sorting and indexing choice.

prefix.q: If you set PRIMARY KEY separately, it must be…
prefix.why: A prefix of the ORDER BY.

count.q: You insert the same order {n} times in {n} INSERTs. How many rows match its key?
count.why: {n}: nothing deduplicates by key in a plain MergeTree.

dedupe.q: Which tool removes duplicate rows by key (eventually)?

3-5.title: Case: EXPLAIN
3-5.summary: Read the funnel and pick the key for a real workload.

brief.title: The slow dashboard
brief.body: A new case: the dashboard is slow. Your evidence is EXPLAIN indexes = 1: for each index stage it shows Parts and Granules selected out of the total. Fewer granules, less work.

limit.q: Exhibit A: SELECT * … ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 1. How many of the 24 granules are read?
limit.why: All 24: total isn't in the key, so the only way to find the biggest is to look at every one. LIMIT doesn't shorten the scan (lazy materialization only defers the other columns).

fix.title: Fix the dashboard
fix.body: Three dashboard queries. Pick the key, run all three and watch EXPLAIN: together they must read 14 granules or fewer.
fix.success: City first: 4 + 4 + 6 = 14. Customer first: 24 + 24 + 1. Case closed!

read.q: EXPLAIN says Granules: {sel}/{total}. What percentage is read?

limit.q: ORDER BY a column outside the key with LIMIT 1 reads…
limit.why: Everything: to know the top row it must see all of them.

pick.q: Most queries filter by city, some by customer. Best ORDER BY?
pick.why: City first: low cardinality, and customer still prunes inside each city.

stage.q: Which EXPLAIN stage shows the sparse index at work?
stage.why: PrimaryKey (Partition is partition pruning, Skip is skipping indexes).

4-1.title: Separate halls
4-1.summary: Partitions: separate halls that never mix.

brief.title: PARTITION BY
brief.body: With PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(date) every month gets its own hall. Each part belongs to one partition, merges never cross partitions, and an INSERT that spans several months creates one part per month. Each part also remembers the min and max of the partition key, so a filter on the date can skip whole parts.
brief.breaks: A partition isn't a building: it's a label on each part. The halls only show which parts share one.

split.title: An insert across months
split.body: One INSERT with orders from September and October arrives. Watch it split into two parts, one per hall.

three.q: An INSERT has orders from 3 different months. How many parts does it create?

cross.q: Could the press merge a part from August with one from September?
cross.no: No: merges stay inside a partition
cross.why: No. Merges only combine parts of the same partition. Watch August's two parts merge with each other.

sept.title: The August report
sept.body: The report filters on August. Pick the column and run it: the other halls should be skipped entirely.
sept.success: EXPLAIN shows it: Partition stage, 1 part of 5. The other months were never opened.

parts.q: One INSERT contains rows from {n} months (monthly partitions). How many parts?

merge.q: Do parts from different partitions ever merge?
merge.why: Never: each partition is merged on its own.

prune.q: How does partition pruning skip parts?
prune.minmax: With each part's min/max of the partition key
prune.name: Only if the query names the partition ID
prune.why: minmax_*.idx per part: any filter on the key columns works.

purpose.why: Data management. Speed comes from the ORDER BY.

4-2.title: Partitioning doesn't speed things up
4-2.summary: Query speed comes from the ORDER BY.

brief.title: A common mix-up
brief.body: Many people partition to make queries fast. The docs are blunt: partitioning does not speed up queries, the ORDER BY does. Partition pruning only helps queries that filter on the partition key. Here the table is partitioned by month and sorted by date.

customer.q: 8 granules spread over 4 months. How many does WHERE customer_id = 4200 read?
customer.why: All 8: the partitions are by month and the order is by date, so nothing tells ClickHouse where customer 4200 is.

fix.title: Make the customer query fast
fix.body: Keep the monthly partitions. Change what really matters and run the customer query: read 4 granules or fewer.
fix.success: ORDER BY customer_id: one granule per month. Same partitions, a quarter of the reading.

speed.q: What makes a filtered query fast?
speed.orderBy: An ORDER BY that matches the filter
speed.why: The ORDER BY (and the sparse index on it).

whenHelps.partitionKey: queries that filter on the partition key
whenHelps.why: Only queries that filter on the partition key's columns.

need.q: The docs' advice on partition keys?
need.often: Often you don't need one; if time-based, monthly
need.why: “In most cases you don't need a partition key.” If you do, monthly.

months.q: Monthly partitions, query for one customer with no date filter, data from {months} months. How many partitions are scanned?
months.why: {months}: without a date filter, every partition.

4-3.title: Too many halls
4-3.summary: Fine-grained partitions multiply parts and hit limits.

brief.title: Day? Customer? Month?
brief.body: An INSERT creates one part per partition it touches. Partition by day and a week of orders is 7 parts; partition by customer and one INSERT can touch hundreds of partitions. ClickHouse refuses an INSERT that touches more than 100 (max_partitions_per_insert_block). Keep the total in the thousands at most.

pick.title: Choose the partition key
pick.body: Insert one week of orders with each key. First get an INSERT rejected, then empty the depot and end with a key that leaves 2 parts or fewer.
pick.success: Monthly: one week, one part. By day: 7 parts per insert. By customer: rejected for touching 480 partitions.

error.q: Which limit rejected the INSERT partitioned by customer?
error.partitions: Too many partitions for a single INSERT block (over 100)
error.why: max_partitions_per_insert_block = 100: one block can't spread over more partitions than that.

key.q: A time-based partition key for most tables?

days.q: Partition by day: one INSERT has orders from {days} days. How many parts?

total.q: How many partitions should a table have at most?
total.why: Keep it under ~1000–10,000: every partition multiplies parts and merges.

4-4.title: Case: delete September
4-4.summary: DROP PARTITION, lightweight DELETE and mutations: three very different costs.

brief.title: A request to forget
brief.body: Final case of the world: legal asks to delete all of a month's orders. There are three ways. ALTER TABLE … DELETE is a mutation: it rewrites every affected part. DELETE FROM is lightweight: it masks the rows, and the space is freed by later merges. DROP PARTITION removes the whole partition at once, as metadata.

guess.q: Which one is cheapest for deleting a whole month?
guess.why: DROP PARTITION: no data is read or rewritten. That's why you design PARTITION BY around how you delete.

compare.title: Try all three
compare.body: Delete each month with a different method and compare: August with a mutation, September with DROP PARTITION, October with a lightweight DELETE.
compare.success: The mutation rewrote box after box. DROP PARTITION was instant. The lightweight DELETE masked October, but its boxes still take space until a merge.

real.title: The real commands
real.body: Mutations run asynchronously (watch system.mutations). Lightweight DELETE has been GA since 23.3.

cheapest.q: Cheapest way to delete a whole month (monthly partitions)?

mutation.q: What does ALTER TABLE … DELETE do to the parts?
mutation.why: It rewrites whole parts, asynchronously: heavy.

space.q: After a lightweight DELETE, when is the disk space freed?
space.merge: When later merges rewrite those parts
space.why: The rows are hidden at once, removed by merges.

design.q: You must delete data month by month. Which PARTITION BY helps most?
design.why: By month: each deletion becomes a DROP PARTITION.

5-1.title: The latest version
5-1.summary: ReplacingMergeTree keeps the newest row per key, eventually.

brief.title: Updates as inserts
brief.body: In this depot each box is one row, with its value printed on it. A ReplacingMergeTree keeps, for every ORDER BY key, the row with the highest ver. To “update” a customer you insert a new version. But the old one only disappears when the two parts merge, at a time nobody chooses.

update.q: Customer 2 moves to Bogotá: we insert version 2. How many rows does SELECT * return now?
update.why: 4: both versions of customer 2 are still there, in different parts. Replacing only happens during merges.

merge.q: The press merges the two parts. How many rows remain?
merge.why: 3: during the merge, the two rows with id = 2 collapse into the one with the highest ver (Bogotá).

moves.title: Two moves and the truth
moves.body: Customers 1 and 3 move too. Insert their new versions, then read the table so it shows only the latest version of each, without waiting for a merge.
moves.success: FINAL merged at read time: one row per customer, the newest. The parts themselves are still unmerged.

when.q: When does ReplacingMergeTree remove older versions?
when.merge: When the parts holding them merge
when.why: During merges, at an unknown time. Until then both versions are stored and returned.

key.q: Which rows count as “the same” for ReplacingMergeTree?
key.orderBy: Rows with the same ORDER BY key
key.primary: Rows with a unique PRIMARY KEY
key.why: The ORDER BY key, per partition. There is no uniqueness constraint.

count.q: You insert {n} versions of the same id in {n} INSERTs and no merge has happened. How many rows does SELECT * show for it?
count.why: {n}: one per part until they merge.

noVer.q: ReplacingMergeTree without a ver column keeps…

brief.title: Reading before the merge
brief.body: A customer complains: the dashboard shows them in two cities. Two tools fix that before any merge. FINAL merges at read time (correct, but it costs more). argMax(city, ver) with GROUP BY picks the newest value with a normal query. And to delete, you insert a version with deleted = 1: FINAL hides it.

ghost.q: Two versions of customer 2, no merge yet. How many rows does WHERE id = 2 return without FINAL?
ghost.why: 2: the old Madrid row and the new Bogotá row. That's the ghost.

delete.q: We insert customer 3 again with deleted = 1. Does customer 3 appear in SELECT * FINAL?
delete.hidden: No: FINAL hides rows marked deleted
delete.shown: Yes, deleted is just another column
delete.why: FINAL keeps the newest version and, being marked deleted, hides it. A plain SELECT still shows it until cleanup merges remove it.

two.title: Two ways to read the truth
two.body: Show the right answer twice: once with FINAL, once with argMax and GROUP BY. Compare them with a plain SELECT.
two.success: Same answer, two routes. FINAL is simpler; argMax is an ordinary aggregation that also works across shards.

final.readTime: Applies the engine's merge logic at read time
final.forces: Forces a real merge on disk
final.why: It merges in the query; the parts on disk stay as they are.

argMax.q: Which function returns the value of the row with the highest version?
argMax.why: argMax(value, ver), grouped by the key.

deleted.q: With ReplacingMergeTree(ver, is_deleted), a row with is_deleted = 1 is hidden…
deleted.final: by FINAL (and removed by cleanup merges)
deleted.why: FINAL hides it; a plain SELECT still sees it until it's cleaned up.

partition.q: Does Replacing deduplicate rows in different partitions?
partition.why: Merges never cross partitions, so neither does deduplication.

5-3.title: Counters that add up
5-3.summary: SummingMergeTree adds numbers per key when parts merge.

brief.title: Pre-aggregated counters
brief.body: A SummingMergeTree adds up the numeric columns of rows with the same key when parts merge, so a counter table stays small. Until then there can be several partial rows per key: always read with sum() and GROUP BY.

rows.q: Page 1 got views in two inserts. How many rows does WHERE page = 1 return before any merge?
rows.why: 2 partial rows (5 and 2). They're only added up when the parts merge.

sum.why: 5 + 2 = 7, merged or not. That's why you query with sum().

zero.q: We insert page 3 with views = −1 (its total becomes 0) and the parts merge. What happens to page 3?
zero.why: When every summed column adds up to 0, SummingMergeTree drops the row.

report.title: A correct report, any time
report.body: More views arrive. Show the views per page correctly while partial rows are still on the shelves.
report.success: sum() with GROUP BY gives the right totals whether or not the press has run.

when.q: When does SummingMergeTree add rows up?
when.why: During merges; so you still sum in queries.

query.q: How should you read a SummingMergeTree table?
query.why: Always aggregate: there may be several partial rows per key.

total.q: Two unmerged rows for a key: {x} and {y}. What does sum() return?

zero.q: After a merge, a key's summed values are all 0. Its row…

5-4.title: Aggregate states
5-4.summary: AggregatingMergeTree stores partial aggregations you can combine.

brief.title: Storing half an aggregation
brief.body: Some results can't just be added: unique users are the classic case. An AggregatingMergeTree stores an aggregate state (here, the set of users seen). You write it with uniqState and read it with uniqMerge, which combines the states without counting anyone twice.

day1.q: Day 1: one part saw users [1, 2, 3] and another saw [2, 3, 4]. What does uniqMerge(users) return for day 1?
day1.why: 4: the states combine into [1, 2, 3, 4]. Adding the counts of each part would say 6.

press.title: States merging
press.body: Watch the press: the two states of day 1 become one, with the union of the users.

count.title: Count the visitors
count.body: Day 2 gets more visits. Show the unique visitors per day correctly, before the parts merge again.
count.success: uniqMerge combines states, so user 5, who visited twice, counts once.

combinators.q: To use AggregatingMergeTree with uniq you write with… and read with…
combinators.why: -State to store the state, -Merge to finish it.

uniq.q: Part A saw {x} users and part B saw {y}, with {shared} in both. Unique users?

direct.q: What do you get selecting an AggregateFunction column directly?
direct.binary: A binary state, not the number
direct.why: A state; finish it with -Merge or finalizeAggregation.

simple.q: For sum, min or max, which lighter type stores plain values?
simple.why: SimpleAggregateFunction: the state is the value itself.

5-5.title: Ins and outs
5-5.summary: CollapsingMergeTree cancels rows with a sign.

brief.title: Cancel and replace
brief.body: CollapsingMergeTree uses a sign column: +1 is a state row, −1 cancels it. To change a value you insert the old row with −1 and the new one with +1. Merges cancel the pairs; queries use sum(sign * x). VersionedCollapsingMergeTree allows any insert order, and CoalescingMergeTree (25.6) keeps the latest non-NULL value per column.

sum.q: User 1 has rows (+1, 5), (−1, 5), (+1, 6). What does sum(sign * views) give?
sum.why: 5 − 5 + 6 = 6: the cancel row removes the old state.

press.title: Pairs cancel
press.body: Watch the press: the +1 and −1 rows of user 1 cancel each other, only (+1, 6) remains.

update.title: Update user 2
update.body: User 2 now has 9 views. Change it the collapsing way, then read the views per user.
update.success: Cancel the old state, insert the new one, and sum with the sign. User 2 shows 9.

sign.q: What does a row with sign = −1 do?
sign.why: It cancels the state row with the same key.

versioned.anyOrder: Rows can arrive in any order (version column)
versioned.why: A version column, so cancel rows needn't follow their states.

coalescing.q: What does CoalescingMergeTree keep per key?
coalescing.perColumn: The latest non-NULL value of each column

6-1.title: Mutations
6-1.summary: ALTER TABLE … UPDATE/DELETE rewrites whole parts.

brief.title: Parts never change
brief.body: Parts are immutable: nobody edits a box in place. So ALTER TABLE … UPDATE or DELETE is a mutation: in the background, every part that holds at least one matching row is rewritten whole as a new part, and the new name gets the mutation version as a suffix. The ALTER returns at once; system.mutations tells you when it is really done.

one.q: Customer 5 moves to Cusco. Each part holds 3 customers. How many rows does the mutation rewrite?
one.why: 3: the whole part all_2_2_0 is rewritten, not just the one row. The new part is all_2_2_0_4 (4 is the mutation version).

three.q: Now three separate ALTERs, one per customer 1, 2 and 3, who all live in the same part. How many rows get rewritten in total?
three.why: 9: each mutation rewrites that 3-row part again. One ALTER with WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3) would rewrite it once. Batch your changes.

purge.title: Purge the cancelled
purge.body: Delete every customer with plan = ''cancelled'' with a mutation. Watch parts_to_do count down in system.mutations, then check the table.
purge.success: Two parts held a cancelled customer, so two parts were rewritten whole. Mutations are for rare, large fixes, not for everyday changes.

cost.q: {n} separate ALTER … UPDATEs each hit the same part of {rows} rows. How many rows are rewritten?
cost.why: {n} × {rows} = {total}: each mutation rewrites the part again.

async.q: The ALTER returned instantly. Where do you check whether it has finished?
async.done: Nowhere: if it returned, it's done
async.why: Mutations are asynchronous by default; system.mutations shows parts_to_do and is_done.

key.q: What happens with ALTER TABLE … UPDATE on an ORDER BY column?
key.error: It's refused: key columns can't be updated
key.fine: It works like any other column
key.why: Key columns can't be updated by a mutation; insert a corrected row instead.

name.q: Part all_2_2_0 is rewritten by mutation 4. Its new name is…
name.why: The mutation version is appended; the level doesn't change because it's not a merge.

6-2.title: Lightweight DELETE
6-2.summary: DELETE FROM hides rows at once; merges remove them later.

brief.title: A mask, not a rewrite
brief.body: DELETE FROM (GA since 23.3) doesn't rewrite parts. It sets a hidden _row_exists mask so the rows disappear from queries at once. The data is still on disk: it's removed for real when the part is merged. Here, masked rows turn pink.

cost.q: DELETE FROM customers WHERE plan = cancelled hits 2 rows in 2 parts. How many rows are rewritten right now?
cost.why: 0: only the mask changes. The rows are hidden, not removed.

space.q: Right after that DELETE, how much disk space was freed?
space.some: The size of the deleted rows
space.all: The size of the parts touched
space.why: None: the rows are still in the parts. The space comes back when those parts merge.

clean.title: Delete and reclaim
clean.body: Delete every customer in Madrid with a lightweight DELETE, then force a merge so the hidden rows actually leave the disk.
clean.success: The DELETE hid the rows at once; the merge wrote them out of the new part. In production you let background merges do it.

how.q: How does a lightweight DELETE remove rows?
how.mask: It marks them in a hidden _row_exists mask
how.rewrite: It rewrites every part at once
how.tombstone: It inserts a row with sign −1
how.why: A mask: queries skip masked rows; merges drop them.

disk.q: When do lightweight-deleted rows leave the disk?
disk.why: On the next merge of that part.

count.q: A table has {total} rows. DELETE FROM hides {gone}. What does SELECT count() return?
count.why: {total} − {gone} = {n}: masked rows are filtered out right away.

best.q: You must delete all of last year's data from a table partitioned by month. The cheapest way?
best.drop: DROP PARTITION, one month at a time
best.why: Dropping a partition removes whole parts: no mask, no rewrite.

6-3.title: Lightweight UPDATE
6-3.summary: UPDATE … SET writes a small patch part (Beta).

brief.title: A patch on top
brief.body: Since 25.8, UPDATE … SET is a lightweight UPDATE (still Beta in 26.9). Instead of rewriting parts it writes a tiny patch part with only the key and the changed columns of the matching rows. Queries apply the patch on read; a later merge absorbs it into the real part. Meant for small changes (up to ~10% of a table).

size.q: UPDATE customers SET plan = pro WHERE id = 4. How many boxes does the patch part carry?
size.why: 2: one row, with its key (id) and the changed column (plan). Nothing else is copied.

read.q: Before any merge, what plan does SELECT show for customer 4?
read.pro: pro (the patch is applied on read)
read.why: The patch is applied while reading, so the new value shows right away.

absorb.title: Patch, then absorb
absorb.body: Move every customer in Lima to the pro plan with a lightweight UPDATE, then force a merge so the patches are absorbed into the parts.
absorb.success: The patch was visible at once and the merge folded it into the data: no part was rewritten just for the update.

what.q: What does a lightweight UPDATE write?
what.patch: A small patch part with the key and the changed columns
what.rewrite: A rewritten copy of every touched part
what.why: A patch part, applied on read and absorbed by merges.

status.q: What is the status of lightweight UPDATE in 26.9?

boxes.q: A lightweight UPDATE changes {changed} column(s) in {rows} rows (key: one column). How many values does the patch hold?

when.q: When does a patch part stop existing?
when.merge: When a merge absorbs it into the data
when.why: Merges apply it to the parts and drop it.

6-4.title: TTL: data with an expiry date
6-4.summary: Expired rows go on merges, not at the instant they expire.

brief.title: A rule, applied late
brief.body: TTL day + INTERVAL 30 DAY says rows expire 30 days after their day. But nothing watches the clock: expired rows are removed by a TTL merge, which runs at most every merge_with_ttl_timeout (4 hours by default). Until then they are still stored and still returned. A part whose rows all expired is dropped whole.

before.q: Today is day 40. Rows with day ≤ 10 have expired, but no TTL merge has run yet. How many rows does SELECT return? (There are 8.)
before.why: 8: TTL doesn't hide rows; it removes them when a merge runs.

merge.q: Now a TTL merge runs. Part 1 (days 1–3) is fully expired, part 2 (8, 25, 38) is partly expired, part 3 (36, 39) is fresh. How many parts remain?
merge.why: 2: part 1 is dropped whole, part 2 is rewritten without day 8 (level +1), part 3 stays.

calendar.title: Keep up with the calendar
calendar.body: Move the calendar to day 70 (new events arrive every 10 days) and leave no expired rows stored.
calendar.success: Rows expire on the calendar but leave on merges. If you need them gone exactly on time, also filter by date in your queries.

when.q: When are expired rows physically removed?
when.select: The next time they are read

expires.q: TTL day + INTERVAL {days} DAY. A row of day {day} expires on day…

dropParts.whole: Only whole parts whose rows all expired
dropParts.why: Only whole parts: cheap, and a good fit for time partitions.

6-5.title: Hot and cold storage
6-5.summary: Move old parts from SSD to S3 with a storage policy and TTL.

brief.title: Disks, volumes, policies
brief.body: A storage policy lists volumes, e.g. a fast SSD (hot) and S3 (cold). TTL … TO VOLUME moves whole parts to the next volume as they age, and when the hot disk gets too full (move_factor = 0.1, under 10% free) parts move too. Queries read every volume transparently; cold data is just slower.

move.q: January's part moves to S3. What happens to its rows?
move.copy: The part is copied as-is to the other disk
move.rewrite: The rows are rewritten and recompressed
move.delete: The rows are deleted from the table
move.why: Moves are part-level copies: same part, another disk.

query.q: SELECT * FROM metrics after the move: what comes back?
query.hot: Only the months on the SSD
query.error: An error until the move is undone
query.why: The table spans both volumes; the query reads both.

months.title: Room for new months
months.body: The SSD fits {cap} monthly parts. Bring in 3 new months without the SSD rejecting any: apply the TTL move to send old months to S3.
months.success: Recent months stay on the fast SSD, old ones live on cheap S3, and the table still answers for all of them.

unit.q: What does tiered storage move between disks?

query.q: Querying a month that lives on S3…

factor.q: move_factor = 0.1 on a {size} GB hot disk: parts start moving when free space drops below how many GB?

actions.q: Which of these is a TTL action?
actions.why: TTL can DELETE, move TO DISK/VOLUME, GROUP BY (roll up) or RECOMPRESS.

map.soonBody: This warehouse is still under construction. More ClickHouse is on the way.

w1.title: Columns
w1.body: Why ClickHouse stores each column on its own: reading only what a query names, and why similar values side by side compress so well.

w2.title: Inserts, parts & merges
w2.body: Every insert becomes an immutable part; background merges fuse them. Batching, async inserts and the famous “Too many parts”.

w3.title: ORDER BY & the sparse index
w3.body: Granules of 8,192 rows, an index with one entry per granule, and why the order of your key decides how much gets read.

w4.title: Partitions
w4.body: Separate halls for managing data: pruning, why partitions don't make queries faster, and the cheapest delete there is.

w5.title: Merge-time engines
w5.body: ReplacingMergeTree, SummingMergeTree, AggregatingMergeTree and CollapsingMergeTree: what happens to rows with the same key when parts merge, and how to read the right answer before they do.

w6.title: Change & expire
w6.body: Mutations, lightweight DELETE and UPDATE, TTL and tiered storage: changing or removing data in immutable parts.
